topic.title: Stratified sampling and estimating populations from samples
topic.subject: maths
topic.examWeightHint: A 3- to 4-mark stratified part in most series, usually the last part of a bigger statistics question (Summer 2023 Q18, Summer 2025 Q22(c), November 2025 Q23(c), Summer 2026 Q20), plus a 4- to 5-mark population-estimate-and-critique question in some (Summer 2024 Q15). The hardest versions take the sample from a subgroup, or from frequencies that must first be read off a histogram.
mustMemorise: Stratum share of the sample = (stratum size ÷ population) × sample size
When the sample is taken from a subgroup, that subgroup's total is the population for the calculation
Answers are whole people, animals or objects; round, and check the parts add to the sample size
If the rounded parts fall short, the extra place goes to the group whose exact value had the largest fractional part
Population estimate: (marked in the second sample ÷ size of that sample) = (number marked ÷ population)
Part of a class = (width of the part ÷ width of the class) × frequency, assuming an even spread
On a histogram, frequency = frequency density × class width
A criticism must name a fault in the method described, and the improvement must repair that fault
notOnThisSpec: Systematic, cluster, quota or multi-stage sampling as named techniques (M4-HD-01 names stratified sampling only)
Standard error, confidence intervals or any measure of sampling uncertainty (A level, not GCSE)
Random number tables and formal randomisation procedures

note.title: Stratified sampling and population estimates
note.subject: maths

mustKnow: Stratum share = (stratum size ÷ population) × sample size
Population estimate: marked in sample ÷ sample size = marked in population ÷ population
Part of a class = (part width ÷ class width) × frequency
Histogram: frequency = frequency density × class width

notOnThisSpec: Systematic, cluster or quota sampling by name
Confidence intervals or standard error (A level, not GCSE)

mustBeAbleTo: Work out how many from each group belong in a stratified sample, and check that the parts add to the sample size
Round a stratum share to a whole person, and decide which group takes an extra place when the rounded parts fall short
Work backwards: find the sample size, or a group's size in the population, from one group's contribution
Take a stratified sample from a subgroup named in the question, using that subgroup's total as the population
Estimate part of a class by proportion of its width, assuming an even spread
Read frequencies off a histogram (frequency density × class width) and then sample from them
Estimate a population from a marked sample and a recapture, giving a whole number of animals
Criticise the sampling method actually described, and give an improvement that repairs that fault
Decide, using the figures given, whether a sample represents a group fairly
sheet.howExamined: M4 (calculator, 2 hours, 100 marks). One item most series, and it moves. A 3- to 4-mark stratified calculation, often the last part of a longer statistics question: Summer 2023 Q18 (complete the table, well answered), Summer 2025 Q22(c) (a sample of five from those waiting longer than six hours — many blank), November 2025 Q23(c) (a sample of 80 taken from frequencies that had to be read off a histogram), Summer 2026 Q19 (a sample of 20 from those above a threshold, 3 marks), with working backwards from one group's count in November 2022 Q21, November 2021 Q24(b) and November 2024 Q21(d), and 'explain why a stratified sample is appropriate' (the key word, representative) in November 2023 Q17 and Summer 2022 Q16. Separately, a 4- to 5-mark population-estimate question with a written critique: Summer 2024 Q15, where 28% got full marks. Schemes read MA1 for the group total, MA1 for the proportion and A1 for the whole-number answer; in the critique each of the fault and the improvement is a separate A1.
traps: Writing the group's size in the population, or stopping at the group's count, instead of scaling it to the sample (Summer 2025 M4 Q22(c): many found the count, then did not know what to do next)
Using the whole table's total when the sample is drawn from a subgroup only; Summer 2025 M4 Q22(c), a sample from those waiting longer than six hours, was left blank by many
Leaving a decimal number of people or animals on the answer line (Summer 2024 M4 Q15)
Turning the proportion upside down, so the population goes on top
Splitting the sample equally between the groups instead of proportionally (November 2023 M4 Q17: the weaker answers gave every group a quarter)

Giving 'the two samples were different sizes' as the fault in a capture-recapture study, the commonest wrong answer in Summer 2024 M4 Q15; that scheme paid marks wearing off, births and deaths, or samples too small, each with its improvement
Listing principles of representativeness when the question hands you numbers to calculate with (Summer 2025 M4 Q18)
Not finding the histogram's frequencies (density × class width) before sampling from them: in November 2025 M4 Q23 most could not work out the density scale, so few reached the sample
Getting two of the three groups right and slipping on the third: add your group sizes back up and check they come to the sample size before you write them on the answer lines (Summer 2023 M4 Q18)

noteBlocks.lede: A sample stands in for a whole population, so it should look like it. A stratified sample does: every group gets the same share of the sample as it has of the population. The same idea, run backwards, estimates a population nobody could count, such as the crabs in a rock pool.
can: Work out each group's share of a stratified sample, in whole people that add up.
Sample from part of a table or a histogram, splitting a class where needed.
Estimate a population by capture-recapture, and name a fault that fits the method.

noteBlocks.md:
A **stratified** sample takes each group in the same proportion as the population. If juniors are 24% of a club, juniors are 24% of the sample. So each group's number in the sample is its fraction of the population, times the sample size:
$$\dfrac{\text{group}}{\text{population}} \times \text{sample size}$$
Then two finishing habits: round each answer to a whole person, and add your numbers up. They must come to the sample size before they go on the answer lines.

noteBlocks.stem: A sports centre has 1250 members: 300 juniors, 550 adults and 400 seniors. A stratified sample of 50 members is taken. How many come from each group?

steps.decision: Juniors are 300 of the 1250 members, and that fraction of the sample is juniors.
The same calculation, group by group: only the top of the fraction changes.
The bottom stays 1250, the whole population, every time.
The check: the three groups make the whole sample.

noteBlocks.title: Stratified sampling
noteBlocks.why: More stratified samples worked at writing speed. Watch it after the steps above.

noteBlocks.prompt: In a stratified sample, how much of the sample does each group get?
options: The same share it has of the population
An equal number from every group
noteBlocks.answer: The same share it has of the population
noteBlocks.explain: Each group's share of the sample matches its share of the population, as See it gave juniors 24% of both.

optionNotes.option: An equal number from every group
optionNotes.why: Equal numbers would make a small group as big in the sample as a large one; each group gets its own share instead.
The sample size is fixed first; each group then gets its fraction of it.

twin.prompt: A school has twice as many pupils in Year 8 as in Year 13. In a stratified sample, how do the two years compare?
options: Year 8 has twice as many as Year 13
The two years have the same number
Year 13 has twice as many as Year 8
twin.answer: Year 8 has twice as many as Year 13
twin.explain: Each year keeps its share, so twice the pupils means twice the places.

optionNotes.option: The two years have the same number
optionNotes.why: That is an equal split, which ignores the sizes. Twice the pupils gives twice the places.

optionNotes.option: Year 13 has twice as many as Year 8
optionNotes.why: That turns the proportion round: the bigger year gets the bigger share.

noteBlocks.explain: $\tfrac{250}{2000} = \tfrac{1}{8}$, and $\tfrac{1}{8}$ of 48 is 6: the calculation of See it's step 1 on new numbers.

noteBlocks.title: A sample should be the population, smaller
noteBlocks.md: A sample is only useful if it looks like the population. Different groups can answer differently, so a group given too many places pulls the results towards its own views. Matching each group's share keeps every group at its true size: the sample is **representative**.

noteBlocks.stem: A school has 900 day pupils and 100 boarders. A sample of 20 pupils is asked about the school day. Compare an equal split with a stratified sample.

steps.working: equal split: 10 day pupils and 10 boarders
steps.decision: Boarders would be half the sample, though they are only a tenth of the school.
Each group takes its own share of the 20.

steps.working: boarders: 10% of the school and 10% of the sample
steps.decision: Only the stratified sample keeps the boarders at their true size, so its results speak for the whole school.

noteBlocks.prompt: A firm has 240 office staff and 60 drivers. A sample of 30 split equally would take 15 drivers. What is wrong with that?
options: Drivers would be half the sample but are a fifth of the firm
A sample of 30 is too small to ask
noteBlocks.answer: Drivers would be half the sample but are a fifth of the firm
noteBlocks.explain: Drivers are $\tfrac{60}{300}$, a fifth of the firm, so a fair sample has 6 drivers, not 15: step 3 of See it kept boarders at their true size the same way.

optionNotes.option: A sample of 30 is too small to ask
optionNotes.why: Size is not the problem here; the split is. Drivers are a fifth of the firm but half of this sample.
Office staff are four fifths of the firm but only half of this sample: they are under-represented.

twin.prompt: A village has 720 adults and 80 children. A sample of 30 split equally would take 15 children. What is wrong with that?
options: Children would be half the sample but are a tenth of the village
Children should not be in the sample
twin.answer: Children would be half the sample but are a tenth of the village
twin.explain: Children are $\tfrac{80}{800}$, a tenth of the village, so a stratified sample of 30 takes 3 children.

optionNotes.option: Children should not be in the sample
optionNotes.why: Every group belongs in the sample, in its own share: here 3 children.
Adults are nine tenths of the village but only half of this sample: under-represented.

noteBlocks.md: Shares rarely come out whole. Round each to the nearest whole person: you cannot sample part of someone. Then add the rounded numbers. If they come to one fewer than the sample size, the extra place goes to the group whose exact share was rounded down the most, the one with the largest decimal part.

Keep the exact shares written down until the check is done, so you can see which group was rounded down most. In November 2023 Q17, the examiners reported, some lost a mark for rounding wrongly or for leaving their answers as decimals.

noteBlocks.stem: A theatre club has 700 members: 107 under 16, 112 aged 16 to 25, 268 aged 26 to 60 and 213 over 60. A stratified sample of 40 is taken. How many come from each group?

steps.decision: Each group over 700, times 40: 107 ÷ 700 × 40 = 6.11, and so on.
Each to the nearest whole person.
One short of 40, so one group needs an extra place.
Its share, 6.40, was rounded down by the most. Now the total is 40.

noteBlocks.prompt: A stratified share works out at 8.6 people. How many go in the sample?
noteBlocks.explain: Round to the nearest whole person, as step 2 of See it did: 8.6 rounds to 9.

twin.prompt: A stratified share works out at 21.4 people. How many go in the sample?
twin.explain: 21.4 rounds down to 21: a whole person, never a decimal.

noteBlocks.prompt: For a sample of 30, four exact shares are 7.2, 9.4, 6.3 and 7.1. Rounded, they add to 29. Which group takes the extra place?
noteBlocks.explain: 9.4 was rounded down by 0.4, more than any other, as 6.40 was in step 4 of See it.

optionNotes.why: 7.2 was rounded down by only 0.2; 9.4 lost 0.4.
6.3 lost 0.3; 9.4 lost more, 0.4.

twin.prompt: For a sample of 30, four exact shares are 12.3, 8.45, 4.15 and 5.1. Rounded, they add to 29. Which group takes the extra place?
twin.explain: 8.45 was rounded down by 0.45, the most of the four.

optionNotes.why: 4.15 lost only 0.15; 8.45 lost 0.45.

noteBlocks.md: Sometimes one group's numbers are given and the rest of the table is missing. Find the fraction sampled from that group, its sample over its size: every group is sampled by the same fraction. Then multiply or divide to fill each gap, and check the totals.
November 2024 Q21(d)(i) gave the number sampled from one class of a histogram and asked for the size of the whole sample; most scored nothing on its sampling parts, the examiners reported.

noteBlocks.stem: A club of 360 members takes a stratified sample. Of the 90 members under 16, 6 are sampled. 135 members are aged 31 to 50, and 5 of the sample are over 50. Find the size of the sample.

steps.decision: Every group is sampled by the same fraction as the under-16s.
Multiply a group's size by the fraction to get its sample.
Going back from a sample to a group, divide by the fraction: times 15.
The last group is what is left of the 360.
Check: 360 × 1/15 is 24 as well.

noteBlocks.prompt: A stratified sample is taken from a population of 2400. A group of 300 provides 7 people. How big is the whole sample?
noteBlocks.explain: The group is $\tfrac{300}{2400} = \tfrac{1}{8}$ of the population, so 7 is an eighth of the sample: $7 \times 8 = 56$, the step-3 move of See it.

steps.decision: The subgroup is the population now; 160 is not used again.
5 of the class's 10 minutes, so half of its 40.
10 of the class's 15 minutes; then add the two pieces.

noteBlocks.prompt: A class $32 < m \le 44$ has frequency 42. Assuming an even spread, how many lie between 38 and 44?
noteBlocks.explain: 38 to 44 is 6 of the class's 12 units, so half of 42, as step 2 of See it halved a class.

twin.prompt: A class $60 < d \le 84$ has frequency 36. Assuming an even spread, how many lie between 60 and 68?
twin.explain: 8 of the class's 24 units: a third of 36.

noteBlocks.prompt: In a survey, 84 people were over 18, and 21 of those were over 60. A stratified sample of 28 is taken from those over 18. How many in the sample are over 60?
noteBlocks.explain: The 84 over 18 are the population here: $\tfrac{21}{84} \times 28 = 7$, with the subgroup's total underneath as in step 4 of See it.

noteBlocks.text: Going further: faults that bend the estimate

noteBlocks.md: A capture-recapture estimate rests on three assumptions: the marks stay on, the marked animals mix back in, and the population does not change between the catches. Each fault breaks one, and you can say which way it pushes the estimate: fewer marked animals in the second catch make it too big.

The Summer 2024 Q15 scheme paid these as a fault and its improvement: samples too small, so catch more; marks worn off, so use a lasting tag; births and deaths, so shorten the gap. The commonest wrong fault, the examiners reported, was that the two samples were different sizes, which is no fault: the method compares fractions.

steps.working: Each group's share of the sample $=$ (group size $\div$ population) $\times$ sample size
steps.decision: Stratified means every group is represented in the same proportion as in the population. Writing the rule once, before any arithmetic, is what turns five calculations into one repeated calculation.

options: Because each group should be the same fraction of the sample as it is of the population
Because every group must contribute the same number of pupils
Because the sample must be the same size as the smallest group
whyMenu.explain: A stratified sample copies the shape of the population. Equal numbers from each group would over-represent the small groups.

steps.decision: The fraction is the group's share of the school; multiplying by 75 turns that share into pupils.
Same calculation, four more times. Keep the decimals visible for now — rounding before the check at the end can lose a pupil.

Pupils are whole people, so each figure is rounded to the nearest whole number. In Summer 2024 the examiners noted candidates who left a decimal number of animals in a population question; the same rule applies here.

options: Because you cannot put 16.2 pupils in a sample
Because the answer must always be even
Because decimals are not allowed in statistics
whyMenu.explain: The thing being counted is people, so the answer has to be a whole number of them.

steps.decision: Add the rounded figures and compare with the sample size. They come to 75, so nothing has to be adjusted. If they had come to 74 or 76, one group would be moved by one — the one whose decimal was closest to the halfway point.

steps.decision: The whole method is one assumption: the marked fish have mixed in, so the proportion marked in a handful is the proportion marked in the lake. Writing the two fractions is the method mark.

options: Because the marked fish are assumed to have spread evenly through the lake
Because the two samples were the same size
whyMenu.explain: Even mixing is what lets a small catch stand for the whole lake. If the marked fish stayed together, the second catch would tell you nothing about the rest.

accepted: marked in the second sample ÷ second sample size = number marked ÷ population

steps.decision: Put the numbers in with the marked counts on top and the totals underneath, on both sides. In Summer 2024 only about a quarter of candidates got this far: most did not recognise the proportion argument.
Cross-multiply and divide. A quick sense check: 4 out of 30 is about one in seven, and 24 is about one seventh of 180.

steps.working: Fault: the marks may have worn off, or the trout may not have mixed back through the lake in two weeks. Improvement: use a tag that lasts, and leave longer between the two catches so the marked fish spread out.
steps.decision: The fault must spoil the estimate, and the improvement must mend it. The Summer 2024 scheme paid marks wearing off, births and deaths, or samples too small; 'the samples were different sizes' was the commonest wrong fault.

parts.stem:
The histogram below is about the heights of plants in a nursery.

Calculate how many plants it represents altogether.

scheme.for: frequency = frequency density × class width used for at least one bar

hints: The height of a bar is frequency density, not frequency.
Multiply each density by the width of its class.
The classes are not all the same width.

commonErrors.feedback: The bar heights have been added as if they were frequencies. On a histogram the area of a bar is the frequency, so multiply each height by its class width first.

parts.stem: A stratified sample of 44 plants is taken from the nursery. Estimate how many plants in the sample have a height of more than 50 cm.

scheme.for: plants over 50 cm: (10/20) × 40 = 20 and 20 from the last bar, total 40

hints: 50 cm falls in the middle of the 40 to 60 class.
Take the part of that bar above 50, then all of the last bar.
Scale the result down to the sample of 44.
parts.workedSolution: Above 50 cm: half of the 40 to 60 bar, $\tfrac{10}{20} \times 40 = 20$, plus all 20 of the 60 to 100 bar, giving $40$ plants. Sample: $\dfrac{40}{220} \times 44 = 8$ plants.

commonErrors.feedback: That is the size of the group in the population, not its share of the sample. Multiply the group's fraction by the sample size; the whole point of the method is to scale down.
Only the last bar was used. 50 cm cuts the 40 to 60 bar in half, so half of that bar's 40 plants belong in the group as well.

parts.stem: Give a reason why your answer to part (b) is only an estimate.

accepted: The individual heights inside each class are not known, so the plants are assumed to be spread evenly across the 40 to 60 class

scheme.for: the data is grouped, so splitting the 40 to 60 bar assumes the heights are spread evenly across the class

hints: What did you assume when you took half of the 40 to 60 bar?
parts.workedSolution: Because the histogram only records how many plants fall in each class, not their individual heights. Taking half of the 40 to 60 bar assumes the heights in that class are spread evenly, which may not be true.

commonErrors.feedback: Repeating the word in the question does not answer it. Name the assumption you made: that the heights are spread evenly inside the class you cut in half.

parts.stem:
The histogram shows the lengths of 120 leaves.

Estimate how many leaves are between 6 cm and 9 cm long.

scheme.for: frequencies of the 4 to 8 and 8 to 10 classes: 10 × 4 = 40 and 15 × 2 = 30

hints: A bar's frequency is density times width.
6 to 8 is half of the 4 to 8 class; 8 to 9 is half of the 8 to 10 class.
parts.workedSolution: The 4 to 8 bar holds $10 \times 4 = 40$ leaves and the 8 to 10 bar holds $15 \times 2 = 30$. From 6 to 8 is half of the first, 20; from 8 to 9 is half of the second, 15. So about $20 + 15 = 35$ leaves.

commonErrors.feedback: Those are bar heights. A bar's frequency is its area: density times class width.
70 is both whole bars. Only part of each class lies between 6 and 9 cm: half of 40 and half of 30.

context.setting: Visitor ages, a stratified sample known only from one group

parts.stem:
The ages, $a$ years, of 378 visitors to a castle were: $0 < a \le 16$: 60; $16 < a \le 30$: 90; $30 < a \le 50$: 120; $50 < a \le 80$: 108.

A stratified sample is taken from all 378 visitors. It contains 15 visitors aged over 16 and up to 30.

Estimate how many visitors in the sample are aged between 40 and 60.
hints: Every group is sampled by the same fraction as the 16 to 30 group.
Split the two classes that the ages 40 and 60 fall inside.
parts.workedSolution: The 16 to 30 group is sampled by $\tfrac{15}{90} = \tfrac{1}{6}$, so every group is. From 40 to 50 is half of the 30 to 50 class, $60$; from 50 to 60 is a third of the 50 to 80 class, $36$. So $96$ visitors are aged 40 to 60, and the sample holds about $96 \times \tfrac{1}{6} = 16$ of them.

commonErrors.feedback: 96 is the number of visitors aged 40 to 60, not their share of the sample. Multiply by the fraction sampled, 1/6.
That takes the whole of both classes, 30 to 80. Only the ages 40 to 60 are wanted: half of one class and a third of the other.

context.setting: A wildlife trust: a vet's stratified sample of its red deer, and an estimate of the roe deer in a wood

parts.stem:
A wildlife trust's register lists 228 adult females, 166 adult males and 106 young red deer, 500 in all. A vet will check a stratified sample of 40 of them.

Work out the number of deer from each group, each rounded to the nearest whole deer.  [3]
hints: Each group over 500, times 40.
Round each to the nearest whole deer.
parts.workedSolution: Adult females $\tfrac{228}{500} \times 40 = 18.24$, adult males $\tfrac{166}{500} \times 40 = 13.28$, young $\tfrac{106}{500} \times 40 = 8.48$: rounded, 18, 13 and 8.

commonErrors.feedback: Those are the register's numbers. Each group's share of the 40 is its fraction of 500, times 40.

parts.stem: Your three numbers add to 39, not 40. Which group should provide the extra deer? Give a reason.  [2]

accepted: The young deer: their exact share, 8.48, was rounded down by the most

scheme.for: because 8.48 has the largest decimal part, so it was rounded down by the most

hints: Look back at the exact shares before rounding.
Which one lost the most when it was rounded down?
parts.workedSolution: The exact shares were 18.24, 13.28 and 8.48. All three were rounded down; 8.48 lost the most, 0.48, so the young deer take the extra place: 18, 13 and 9, which make 40.

commonErrors.feedback: The extra place goes by the decimal parts, not by the size of the group. 8.48, for the young deer, was rounded down by the most.

parts.stem:
The trust also estimates the roe deer in a wood. 45 roe deer are tagged and released. Later 56 roe deer are seen, and 8 of them are tagged.

Estimate the number of roe deer in the wood.  [2]
hints: The tagged fraction of the second sighting matches the tagged fraction of the wood.
parts.workedSolution: $\dfrac{8}{56} = \dfrac{45}{N}$, so $N = \dfrac{45 \times 56}{8} = 315$ roe deer.

commonErrors.feedback: The fraction is upside down. The tagged count over the sighting size equals the number tagged over the population.
Adding and taking away the counts does not use the proportion. Write marked over total on both sides.

parts.stem: State one fault with this method of estimating the number of roe deer, and suggest how it could be improved.  [2]

accepted: The tags may fall off, so tagged deer are counted as untagged; use a longer-lasting tag
The samples are too small; see more deer each time

scheme.for: a fault in the procedure: tags falling off, deer not mixing back, births and deaths between the counts, or samples too small
reject: the two samples were different sizes

scheme.for: an improvement that mends the stated fault

hints: What could make a tagged deer look untagged, or change the herd between the counts?
parts.workedSolution: Fault: tags may fall off between the two counts, so tagged deer are recorded as untagged and the estimate is too big. Improvement: use a tag that lasts until the second count.

commonErrors.feedback: The two counts need not be the same size: the method compares fractions. The Summer 2024 examiners named this as the commonest wrong fault.

findTheMistake.stem: Orla was asked: a village of 1200 people contains 320 people aged under 18. A stratified sample of 75 people is taken. How many should be under 18? Her working:
findTheMistake.whatWentWrong: The group's share of the village was worked out correctly and then the group's own size was written on the answer line. The share still has to be turned into people in the sample by multiplying by 75.
findTheMistake.feedback: The fraction is right and earns the method mark. The last step is the one that makes it a sample: multiply the fraction by the sample size. A sample of 75 cannot contain 320 people, and that check takes a second. In Summer 2025 Q22(c) many found the group's count and then did not scale it to the sample, the examiners reported.

findTheMistake.stem: Finn was asked to estimate a rabbit population. 18 rabbits were caught, marked and released; later 28 rabbits were caught and 5 were marked. His working:
findTheMistake.whatWentWrong: Every line of the proportion and the arithmetic is correct. The answer line still reports 0.8 of a rabbit; a population is a whole number of animals.
findTheMistake.feedback: Both method marks stand: the proportion is set up exactly as the scheme wants and the calculation is right. Only the final accuracy mark is at risk, and one word — 'about 101 rabbits' — protects it. Summer 2024 M4 Q15: some candidates who found the estimate left a decimal number of animals and lost that mark.

findTheMistake.stem: Meabh was asked: a table shows 250 journeys, of which 60 took over 40 minutes and 40 took over 60 minutes. A stratified sample of 20 journeys is taken **from those over 40 minutes**. How many of the sample took over 60 minutes? Her working:
findTheMistake.whatWentWrong: The sample is drawn only from the 60 journeys over 40 minutes, so 60 is the population for this calculation, not 250. Using the whole table makes the answer far too small.
correction: The sample comes from the 60 journeys over 40 minutes
findTheMistake.feedback: The shape of the working is exactly right, which is worth noticing — the rule was applied correctly to the wrong population. Read the sampling sentence twice and underline the words that say where the sample comes from, then write that total down before anything else. Summer 2025 M4 Q22(c) asked for a sample from those waiting longer than six hours, and many left it blank.

prompts.prompt: In a stratified sample, what fraction of the sample comes from a group?
A stratified share works out at 9.6 people. What do you write?
The sample comes from a subgroup only. Which total goes underneath?
prompts.answer: The subgroup's total, not the whole table's.

prompts.prompt: In capture-recapture, which fraction matches the fraction of the population that is marked?
prompts.answer: The marked fraction of the second catch.

prompts.prompt: Two catches of different sizes: is that a capture-recapture fault?
Which word earns the mark for saying a stratified sample suits a survey?
Marks wear off between the catches. Is the estimate too big or too small?
prompts.answer: Too big: fewer marked animals are recaught.

findings.asked: Work out the numbers from each age group in a stratified sample.
findings.wentWrong: Mostly full marks; the rest were blank or wrong throughout, with the occasional slip in one age group only.
findings.rule: Group share of the sample = group size / population x sample size.

findings.asked: Estimate a population from a marked sample and a second sample, then give one fault and one improvement of the method.
findings.wentWrong: Only about a quarter got the estimate; most did not recognise the proportion argument. Some who did left a decimal number of animals. Critiques were often generic (sample size) rather than about the method described.
findings.fullMarkAnswersDid: Set the proportion marked in the second sample equal to the proportion marked in the population, solved, and rounded to a whole number; then criticised the specific procedure in the question.
findings.rule: Marked in sample / sample size = marked in population / population; give whole animals and a fault tied to the given method.

findings.asked: Reason about whether a sample of a given size, with a given percentage, represents a population.
findings.wentWrong: Even strong candidates overthought it and listed memorised points about representativeness. Those who calculated 30% of 142 and compared it with the population got the marks.
findings.fullMarkAnswersDid: Did the one calculation the data allowed and compared numbers, not principles.
findings.rule: When numbers are given, calculate with them; a reasoning mark comes from the specific data.

findings.asked: Stratified sample using frequencies read from a histogram.
